strengths: Significance: Accelerating autoregressive video diffusion on consumer GPUs is useful. Table 1 reports a favorable practical tradeoff: 1.30× and 1.19× end-to-end speedups on Self Forcing and LongLive, respectively, while maintaining competitive aggregate VBench scores.

Originality: Allocating greater attention budgets to early chunks and combining frame retrieval with block selection is a plausible adaptation of sparse attention to autoregressive generation. Figure 2 provides an intuitive illustration of early-chunk sensitivity.

Empirical merits: Evaluation includes two model checkpoints, several sparse-attention baselines, all 16 VBench dimensions, component ablations, and measured GPU latency. Table 2 shows that adding HSA substantially improves dynamic degree over CAG alone, from 37.5 to 66.7.

Presentation and limitations: The overview and qualitative comparisons communicate the approach effectively. The manuscript explicitly acknowledges its restriction to 1.3B models and hardware portability limitations. No material research-ethics violation is apparent from the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theoretical justification: Appendix B analyzes denoising within a fixed chunk and fixed conditioning; it does not establish that generating the next chunk is equivalent to continuing denoising the previous chunk, or quantify propagation through generated conditioning. Consequently, it does not derive the chunk-dependent allocation in Eq. (5). Neither the relationship between sparsity and score error nor the mapping from chunk index to the effective step count is established. Calling CAG a quantitative allocation based on global accumulation error therefore overstates the result.

Soundness—the bound itself is inadequately justified: Appendix B assumes an ideal Gaussian reverse kernel with the same covariance without showing that its endpoint equals the true conditional data distribution. The transfer of the cited convergence theorem to this denoising/re-noising sampler is asserted without verifying its conditions. Equation (4) also has a d² dependence where Eq. (21) has d, while noise level and step count are used inconsistently. These issues go beyond a missing proof detail.

Soundness—complexity claim: HSA is repeatedly described as having fixed complexity independent of history length, but Eq. (8) scores every historical frame. Appendix A additionally sets the selected-block count proportional to (1−s_i) times the full historical length, which grows under the stated schedule and can eventually exceed the capacity of a fixed retrieved-frame set. The implementation needs a clear cap/budget policy and an accurate complexity analysis.

Evaluation—insufficient isolation of the contribution: Table 2 lacks an HSA-only condition and comparisons against simpler budget-matched schedules, particularly a dense first chunk followed by constant sparsity. Appendix A reveals that the first chunk is explicitly kept dense, so the benefit of progressive CAG allocation is not separated from this intervention. An equally fine-tuned dense control is also needed to attribute improvements over the pretrained dense model to sparsity.

Evaluation—claims exceed the evidence: Quality evaluation covers only five-second videos, which does not substantiate claims about long-range consistency, history forgetting, or long-duration synthesis. The aggregate improvements over dense attention are small and reported without seed variability or uncertainty; several individual metrics decline. Figure 6 usefully separates acceleration components, but the combined FP8/LightVAE deployment has no corresponding quantitative quality evaluation. Average throughput alone also leaves streaming startup and per-chunk latency uncharacterized.

Reproducibility: Reporting 2,000 fine-tuning iterations is insufficient without the training data, objective, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and trainable-parameter configuration. The exact α_i schedule, treatment of the dense first chunk in Eq. (6), and allocation of selected blocks across retrieved frames are unclear. Equation (9) selects top-k historical frames plus the current chunk, whereas Appendix A describes selection within six frames. These ambiguities affect faithful implementation; a future code-release promise does not resolve them.

Presentation and originality: Equations (3) and (13) multiply logits by a binary mask, which leaves excluded entries with nonzero softmax probability rather than excluding them. Although the described kernel may implement masking correctly, the formal definitions require correction. The individual pooling, retrieval, and block-selection mechanisms build closely on existing sparse-attention ideas; the potentially useful novelty is their autoregressive allocation and integration, whose benefit needs stronger controlled evidence.

strengths: Significance: Accelerating autoregressive video diffusion on consumer GPUs is useful. Table 1 reports practical end-to-end speedups of 1.30× on Self Forcing and 1.19× on LongLive, with aggregate VBench scores slightly above their dense baselines.

Originality: Allocating more attention to early chunks and combining historical-frame retrieval with block selection is a sensible adaptation to autoregressive generation. Figure 2 provides an illustrative motivation for protecting early chunks.

Empirical evidence: The evaluation includes two model backbones, several sparse-attention baselines, all 16 VBench dimensions, component ablations, and runtime decomposition. Table 2 shows that adding HSA improves dynamic degree from 37.5 to 66.7 and total score from 83.2 to 84.5.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline and qualitative comparisons are generally understandable. Appendix D explicitly acknowledges the restriction to 1.3B models and kernel portability limitations. No material research-ethics violation is apparent from the manuscript.
weaknesses: Soundness—CAG's central theoretical justification is unsupported. Section 4.1 treats generating a new chunk from fresh noise, conditioned on previous chunks, as additional denoising of the preceding chunk. Appendix B only studies a fixed conditional denoising chain; it does not establish this equivalence or bound error propagation across generated contexts. It also supplies no relationship between attention sparsity and score error that would derive Equation 5. Consequently, CAG remains a heuristic rather than the claimed quantitative allocation based on global accumulation error.

Soundness—the proof contains additional gaps. An exact denoiser does not automatically make the stipulated Gaussian re-noising transition an exact reverse kernel with the true data distribution as its endpoint. The conditions needed to transfer the cited diffusion convergence result to this few-step sampler are not established. Equation 4 uses d² while Equation 21 uses d, and t alternates between noise level and sampling-step count. These inconsistencies materially weaken the claimed guarantee.

Soundness and scalability: The claim that HSA has complexity independent of historical length is inaccurate for the full procedure: Equation 8 scores every historical frame. Moreover, Appendix A specifies a selected-block budget proportional to (1−s_i)i, which generally grows with history under the stated schedule, despite retrieval from a fixed number of frames. The manuscript needs a consistent complexity analysis and an explicit rule for when the requested block budget exceeds the retrieved candidates.

Evaluation does not isolate the proposed allocation strategy. Table 2 omits HSA without CAG and comparisons against simpler schedules, particularly a dense first chunk followed by constant sparsity. Appendix A already applies a special dense-first-chunk rule, so its contribution cannot be separated from CAG. Baseline adaptation also removes STA's dense early-timestep safeguard without evaluating alternatives. These omissions leave the necessity and comparative advantage of the proposed schedule uncertain.

Significance claims exceed the evidence. Quantitative evaluation covers five-second videos, which does not substantiate claims about long-duration consistency, history forgetting, or sustained streaming. The 19.7 FPS configuration additionally uses FP8 and LightVAE, but its quality is not quantitatively evaluated. Average throughput alone does not establish interactive streaming performance without startup and per-chunk latency measurements.

Reproducibility and statistical support are inadequate. The paper specifies 2,000 fine-tuning iterations but omits the training data, objective, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and detailed parameter-update configuration. The exact mapping from chunk index to α_i is unspecified, and the code-release statement has no usable link. Evaluation sample counts, seeds, uncertainty estimates, and timing methodology are also absent. The 0.4–0.7-point gains over dense attention therefore do not establish statistically reliable quality improvement, especially without an equally fine-tuned dense control.

Presentation includes consequential mathematical errors: Equations 3 and 13 multiply logits by a binary mask before softmax, which assigns masked entries nonzero probability rather than excluding them. Although the described kernel may implement masking correctly, the equations do not specify that computation. Overall, the promising engineering results do not outweigh the unresolved theoretical, experimental, and reproducibility deficiencies.

strengths: Significance: Accelerating autoregressive video diffusion on consumer GPUs is useful. Table 1 reports meaningful end-to-end speedups of 1.30× on Self Forcing and 1.19× on LongLive, while preserving or improving aggregate VBench scores.

Originality: Protecting early chunks from aggressive sparsification and retrieving historical context through frame-level followed by block-level selection form a sensible AR-specific contribution. The main novelty lies in this combination and its motivating observations.

Empirical merits: The evaluation includes two model variants, several sparse-attention baselines, detailed VBench dimensions, component ablations, and runtime decomposition. Table 2 shows that HSA substantially improves dynamic degree over CAG alone, from 37.5 to 66.7.

Presentation and limitations: The overall architecture and qualitative motivation are understandable. The authors appropriately acknowledge evaluation on only 1.3B models and kernel portability limitations. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theoretical justification is unsupported. Section 4.1 treats generating a new chunk conditioned on previous chunks as continuing their denoising trajectory. Appendix B instead analyzes denoising a single chunk under fixed conditioning; it does not establish this cross-chunk equivalence, characterize propagation of sparsity errors, or derive the allocation in Eq. (5). Each chunk starts from fresh noise, so a bound improving with denoising steps does not directly imply improvement with chunk index.

The theoretical details also require correction. Appendix B assumes that an ideal Gaussian mean-map chain corresponds to the true conditional data distribution without establishing this property or its discretization error. The claimed bound changes its dimension dependence from d² in Eq. (4) to d in Eq. (21), and logarithmic factors are incorrectly described as constants that do not affect asymptotic complexity. These issues undermine the claimed quantitative foundation for CAG.

The history-independent complexity claim in Section 4.2 is not supported by the algorithm as written. Frame retrieval scores every historical frame in Eq. (8), so selection cost grows with history. Appendix A additionally specifies a selected-block budget proportional to chunk index, which eventually exceeds the capacity of a fixed retrieved-frame set unless capped. Neither the cap nor the resulting sparsity behavior is specified. Evaluation only on five-second videos does not substantiate long-duration consistency or sustained streaming efficiency.

The ablations do not isolate the value of the proposed CAG schedule. Table 2 lacks HSA without CAG and a simple dense-first-chunk/constant-sparsity control, although Appendix A makes the first chunk dense. Comparisons against alternative schedules at matched computation are needed to establish whether the proposed allocation adds value beyond protecting the first chunk.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the essential post-training stage. The paper gives 2,000 iterations but omits the training data, objective, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and detailed parameter-update configuration. The operational mapping from chunk index to α_i is unclear, and block selection is described per frame in Eq. (11) but through a total budget in Appendix A. A promised future code release does not resolve these ambiguities.

Evaluation does not convincingly establish quality superiority. The aggregate improvements over dense attention are small, with no repeated-seed uncertainty, and the sparse model receives additional training without an equivalently trained dense control. Baseline adaptations also need stronger validation: STA loses its original dense-timestep protection, and VMoBA performs exceptionally poorly on LongLive. Matched latency–quality curves would better support broad superiority claims.

The combined deployment result lacks quality validation. Figure 6 clearly separates the runtime contributions of LightVAE, FP8, and sparse attention, but the fully accelerated configuration has no corresponding quantitative quality results. Calling the added optimizations lossless is insufficient evidence. Equations (3) and (13) also incorrectly implement masking by multiplying logits by a binary mask, which leaves excluded entries with nonzero softmax probability.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in autoregressive video diffusion. Sparse attention alone provides useful measured speedups: 1.30× on Self Forcing and 1.19× on LongLive in Table 1, with additional measurements across RTX 5090, A100, and H100.

Originality: Combining an allocation of larger attention budgets to early chunks with query-dependent frame retrieval is a useful adaptation of sparse attention to autoregressive generation. The observation that early-chunk degradation can propagate through subsequent generation provides a plausible empirical motivation.

Empirical merits: Evaluation covers three model variants, short and longer videos, several sparse-attention baselines, and detailed VBench dimensions. Table 3 demonstrates substantial recovery over naive sparse attention, while Table 4 examines sensitivity to the frame-retrieval budget.

Presentation and limitations: The overall architecture is understandable, and the qualitative examples help explain the intended benefits. Appendix J candidly acknowledges model-scale restrictions and remaining artifacts; Appendix H appropriately distinguishes attention acceleration from memory reductions supplied by other deployment components.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theoretical justification: Appendix C analyzes denoising within one chunk under fixed conditioning. It does not establish the key claim that generating a new chunk is equivalent to continuing denoising the previous chunk for another T steps. Each chunk starts from fresh Gaussian noise and represents different content. Consequently, the within-chunk sampling bound does not justify an error decay with chunk index or the proposed chunkwise sparsity schedule. No relationship between attention sparsity and score-estimation error is derived, and the mapping from chunk index to alpha_i in Eq. (5) is not explicitly specified.

Soundness—additional mathematical problems: Eq. (19) treats the endpoint of an ideal Gaussian mean-map chain as the true conditional data distribution without establishing that equivalence or including its discretization error. The subsequent appeal to Li et al. does not verify the required schedule and regularity assumptions for this sampler. Furthermore, the dimension dependence changes from d² in Eq. (4) to d in Eq. (21). Eqs. (3) and (13) multiply logits by a binary mask before softmax, which assigns nonzero probability to excluded entries rather than implementing the described sparse attention.

Experimental attribution: Table 3 lacks a dense-first-chunk followed by constant-sparsity control, alternative increasing schedules, and an HSA-only variant at matched compute. These comparisons are particularly important because the paper itself identifies the first chunk as unusually sensitive. The current ablation cannot establish the benefit of the specific CAG schedule beyond preserving that initial chunk. CAG also reduces Dynamic Degree from 46.4 to 37.5 before HSA is added.

Evidence for quality claims: LIGHT FORCING receives 2,000 additional training iterations, but an equivalently trained dense control is not reported. The small total-score gains over dense attention therefore cannot be attributed specifically to sparsity. Evaluation sample counts, repeated-run variability, and uncertainty estimates are not provided. Claims of lossless performance are also stronger than the dimension-level results: semantic scores decrease on all three model variants, and some consistency and aesthetic metrics decline.

Reproducibility: The manuscript omits essential post-training information, including the training data, objective, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and training cost. The supplied PDF presents code, model, and Docker references as links or footnote markers without usable destinations. Baseline hyperparameters and deployment timings are helpful, but they do not resolve the missing specification of how to reproduce the trained models.

Scalability and comparison scope: HSA's frame-scoring stage in Eq. (8) still examines all candidate historical frames, so the complete attention procedure is not independent of history length as claimed. The unchanged peak memory in Table 11 also provides no evidence of bounded cache growth. Evaluation stops at 15 seconds, and the long-video quantitative comparison includes only the dense baseline, leaving the claimed advantage over sliding-window or sink-based history handling insufficiently tested.

Deployment claims: The 2–3× end-to-end gains combine sparse attention with FP8, kernel fusion, and a replacement VAE. Their separate latency contributions are reported, but corresponding quality measurements for the complete optimized stack are missing. Thus, the manuscript does not establish that its strongest speed and quality claims hold simultaneously. No material ethical violation is evident, although missing training-data provenance also limits assessment of responsible data use.

strengths: Significance: Accelerating autoregressive video diffusion is a useful practical objective. Table 1 reports competitive quality with meaningful end-to-end improvements: Self Forcing latency decreases from 9.61s to 7.39s, and LongLive from 10.47s to 8.81s.

Originality: Protecting early chunks from aggressive sparsification and retrieving historical context separately for each query block constitute a sensible adaptation to autoregressive generation. Figure 2 provides an intuitive motivation for treating early chunks differently.

Empirical evidence: Evaluation covers three 1.3B models, two video durations, several sparse-attention baselines, and three GPU architectures. Full per-dimension benchmark results and incremental deployment measurements are useful. Table 3 shows a substantial recovery from naive sparse attention to the complete method.

Presentation and limitations: The overall pipeline is understandable, and the appendix candidly acknowledges model-scale restrictions and residual artifacts. The memory analysis appropriately reports that sparse attention alone does not reduce measured peak memory.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theoretical claim is unsupported: Section 4.1 treats generating a new chunk as continuing denoising the preceding chunk for additional steps. Appendix C instead analyzes a single chunk with fixed conditioning; it does not establish this equivalence or control error propagation through generated histories. Every chunk starts from fresh Gaussian noise and receives the same number of denoising steps. Consequently, the single-chunk bound does not establish decreasing error with chunk index, quantify contributions to global rollout error, or derive the allocation in Eq. (5). No relationship between attention sparsity and score-estimation error is established.

Soundness—the proof has additional gaps: Appendix C assumes that an ideal Gaussian mean-map kernel yields the true conditional data distribution, without establishing this for the proposed denoise-and-renoise sampler. The imported convergence assumptions are not verified for the actual few-step generator. Moreover, Eq. (4) has a d² dependence whereas Eq. (21) has d, and the stated KL scaling does not transparently imply the latter expression. These issues materially weaken the claimed theoretical foundation.

Causal evaluation is incomplete: Table 3 lacks HSA alone and a dense-first-chunk baseline followed by constant sparsity. These controls are needed to determine whether the proposed growth schedule improves on simply preserving the visual anchor. Alternative schedules at matched compute and latency are also missing. CAG alone increases total score from 82.8 to 83.2 but decreases dynamic degree from 46.4 to 37.5; the subsequent HSA improvement therefore does not establish the necessity of the specific CAG schedule.

Claims exceed the quality evidence: Improvements over dense attention are small in aggregate and lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-seed results. Semantic scores decrease on all three evaluated models, and LongLive also loses aesthetic quality, motion smoothness, and background consistency. Furthermore, LIGHT FORCING receives 2,000 additional training iterations without a matched dense fine-tuning control. Thus, claims of lossless performance or quality gains attributable specifically to sparsity are not established. The 15-second evaluation compares only with dense attention and does not substantiate superiority over alternative long-context strategies.

Efficiency claims need qualification: HSA's frame retrieval scores every candidate historical frame in Eq. (8), so total selection cost still grows with history; fixed retained attention does not imply history-independent overall complexity. The approximately 2–3× deployment gains also include FP8, fused operators, and a replacement VAE. Although the incremental timing breakdown is helpful, benchmark quality for the complete optimized stack is not reported, leaving the headline speed–quality tradeoff insufficiently verified.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the training-dependent results: The manuscript specifies iteration counts and several inference settings but omits the training data, objective, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and detailed training configuration. The exact chunk-index dependence of α_i is also not specified by saying it scales as 1/√T. Code, checkpoint, and Docker references appear as link placeholders or empty footnotes in the supplied manuscript, preventing verification through those resources. Training-data provenance is consequently also unclear, although no concrete ethical violation is evident.

Mathematical presentation needs correction: Eqs. (3) and (13) multiply attention logits by a binary mask before softmax. This assigns nonzero probability to excluded positions rather than removing them. The prose describes skipping inactive tiles, suggesting a notation error, but the formal definition should use exclusion or an additive negative-infinity mask. Overall, the practical merits do not outweigh the unresolved theoretical, evidential, and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in autoregressive video diffusion. Table 1 reports useful speed–quality tradeoffs: Self Forcing latency falls from 9.61s to 7.39s while VBench increases from 84.1 to 84.5; LongLive shows similar benefits.

Originality: Protecting early chunks from approximation error and retrieving historical context separately for each query block form a sensible adaptation of sparse attention to autoregressive generation. Figure 2 provides an intuitive motivation for treating chunks differently.

Empirical coverage: Experiments include three pretrained models, multiple sparse-attention baselines, detailed benchmark dimensions, and three GPU platforms. Table 10 separates sparse-attention gains from additional deployment optimizations, and Table 11 transparently reports that sparse attention alone does not reduce peak memory.

Presentation and limitations: The overall architecture and coarse-to-fine retrieval pipeline are understandable. Appendix J appropriately acknowledges the restriction to 1.3B models, remaining artifacts, and hardware-dependent acceleration. No concrete ethical violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—CAG's central theoretical justification is unsupported. Appendix C analyzes denoising within one chunk under fixed conditioning; it does not establish that generating a different subsequent chunk constitutes additional denoising of the preceding chunk. Consequently, the bound in denoising-step count T does not establish decreasing error with chunk index i or justify the sparsity schedule in Eq. (5). Neither the dependence of score error on sparsity nor an explicit computable definition of alpha_i is supplied. Eq. (4) and Eq. (21) also disagree on dimensional dependence, using d² and d respectively.

Causal attribution is incomplete. Table 3 lacks both an HSA-only variant and a dense-first-chunk baseline with constant sparsity thereafter. It therefore does not establish whether progressive CAG allocation improves over simply protecting the first chunk. Component latencies and matched realized FLOPs are also absent. This matters because adding CAG reduces dynamic degree from 46.4 to 37.5, whereas the subsequent HSA addition produces the largest recovery.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the required post-training. Section 5.1 specifies 2,000 iterations but does not document the training data, objective, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, or detailed parameter-update configuration. Reporting code availability and selected inference hyperparameters does not replace these essential methodological details.

Quality claims exceed the evidence. The small aggregate improvements lack repeated-seed results or uncertainty estimates, and the dense baseline does not receive a matched additional-training control. Semantic scores decrease on all three evaluated models, with other individual regressions visible in the detailed tables. These results support a promising tradeoff more clearly than 'lossless performance.' The combined FP8/LightVAE deployment stack also lacks corresponding quantitative quality evaluation.

Scalability is overstated. Eq. (8) scores every candidate historical frame, so frame retrieval grows with history length even if the final selected attention budget is fixed. The complete HSA procedure therefore does not have history-independent complexity as claimed. Evaluation to only 15 seconds, with no sparse competitors in the long-video table, does not establish the broader long-range robustness claim.

Technical presentation needs correction: Eqs. (3) and (13) multiply attention logits by a binary mask before softmax, which gives excluded entries nonzero probability rather than removing them. The intended skipped-tile implementation may be correct, but the equations are not. Together with the theoretical and experimental gaps above, this prevents acceptance despite the practical promise.
